title: Hybrid Search and Reranking
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Hybrid Search and Reranking ##### nDCG 0.61 to 0.89 without touching the embedding model An e-commerce search team in Bengaluru had spent two months on embedding models. They had tried `all-mpnet-base-v2`, `bge-large-en`, OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-large`, and a fine-tuned variant of their own. nDCG@10 moved from 0.58 to 0.61. Then they added BM25 alongside dense retrieval and fused the results with RRF. **0.74.** Then they added a cross-encoder reranker over the top 30 candidates. **0.89.** Two weeks of work beat two months of embedding tuning by 28 points. The reason is structural. Their queries included product codes (`WH-4471-BLK`), brand names, and exact model numbers — strings that carry no semantic content and embed to essentially nothing. No embedding model can fix that, because the information is lexical, not semantic. And the reranker fixed a different problem entirely: the right result was often retrieved at position 12, where the generator never saw it. **Retrieval quality is usually limited by architecture, not by the embedding model.** Today is the two architectural changes with the highest return. ##### Two retrieval paradigms ```mermaid flowchart TD Q["Query: 'WH-4471 warranty period'"] --> S["Sparse / BM25"] Q --> D["Dense / embeddings"] S --> S1["Matches: WH-4471 exactly
Misses: 'guarantee duration'"] D --> D1["Matches: 'guarantee duration'
Misses: WH-4471"] S1 --> F["Reciprocal Rank Fusion"] D1 --> F F --> R["Cross-encoder rerank
top 30 → top 5"] R --> O["Final results"] ``` | | Sparse (BM25) | Dense (embeddings) | |---|---|---| | Matches | Exact terms | Meaning | | Product codes, IDs | **Excellent** | Poor | | Synonyms | Poor | **Excellent** | | Rare technical terms | **Excellent** | Depends on training | | Typos | Poor | **Tolerant** | | Long queries | Degrades | Good | | Explainability | **You see the matched terms** | Opaque | | Index cost | Low | Higher | | Domain adaptation | Immediate | Needs fine-tuning | **They fail on disjoint query sets**, which is exactly why fusing them works so well. ##### BM25 Not a heuristic — a principled probabilistic ranking function, and still the strongest single sparse method after thirty years. $$\text{BM25}(q, d) = \sum_{t \in q} \text{IDF}(t) \cdot \frac{f(t,d) \cdot (k_1 + 1)}{f(t,d) + k_1 \cdot \left(1 - b + b \cdot \frac{|d|}{\text{avgdl}}\right)}$$ The two mechanisms that matter: **Term-frequency saturation** via `k_1`. Unlike TF-IDF, a term appearing 50 times does not score 50× a term appearing once — the contribution saturates. This prevents keyword-stuffed documents from dominating. **Length normalisation** via `b`. Longer documents naturally contain more terms; `b=0.75` partially corrects for that without over-penalising genuinely comprehensive documents. ```python import re import math from collections import Counter class BM25: def __init__(self, corpus_tokens, k1=1.5, b=0.75): self.k1, self.b = k1, b self.corpus = corpus_tokens self.N = len(corpus_tokens) self.doc_lens = [len(d) for d in corpus_tokens] self.avgdl = sum(self.doc_lens) / max(self.N, 1) self.df = Counter() for doc in corpus_tokens: self.df.update(set(doc)) self.idf = { t: math.log((self.N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5) + 1.0) for t, n in self.df.items() } self.tf = [Counter(doc) for doc in corpus_tokens] def score(self, query_tokens, doc_idx): s, tf, dl = 0.0, self.tf[doc_idx], self.doc_lens[doc_idx] for t in query_tokens: if t not in tf: continue f = tf[t] denom = f + self.k1 * (1 - self.b + self.b * dl / self.avgdl) s += self.idf.get(t, 0.0) * f * (self.k1 + 1) / denom return s def search(self, query_tokens, k=10): scores = [(i, self.score(query_tokens, i)) for i in range(self.N)] return sorted(scores, key=lambda x: -x[1])[:k] TOKEN_RE = re.compile(r"[a-z0-9]+(?:[-_][a-z0-9]+)*", re.IGNORECASE) def tokenize(text: str) -> list[str]: """Preserve hyphenated identifiers like WH-4471-BLK as single tokens.""" return [t.lower() for t in TOKEN_RE.findall(text)] ``` **That tokenizer regex is doing real work.** A naive `\w+` splits `WH-4471-BLK` into three tokens, and the exact-match advantage evaporates. Preserving hyphenated and underscored identifiers is the single most important BM25 tuning decision for technical corpora. **Parameter guidance:** `k1` between 1.2 and 2.0 (higher favours term frequency); `b` between 0.5 and 0.8 (lower for corpora with wildly varying document lengths). Defaults of 1.5 and 0.75 are fine for most cases. **Production options:** Elasticsearch and OpenSearch implement BM25 natively with proper inverted indexes; `rank_bm25` is fine up to a few hundred thousand documents in memory; Postgres full-text search is a reasonable choice if you already run Postgres. ##### Reciprocal Rank Fusion The problem with combining BM25 and dense scores directly: BM25 scores are unbounded and corpus-dependent, cosine similarities live in [−1, 1]. Any weighted sum requires per-corpus tuning that breaks whenever your data changes. **RRF uses only ranks:** $$\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)}$$ ```python def reciprocal_rank_fusion(ranked_lists, weights=None, k=60, top_n=None): """ranked_lists: {name: [doc_id, ...]} in descending relevance.""" weights = weights or {name: 1.0 for name in ranked_lists} scores, sources = {}, {} for name, ranking in ranked_lists.items(): w = weights.get(name, 1.0) for rank, doc_id in enumerate(ranking, start=1): scores[doc_id] = scores.get(doc_id, 0.0) + w / (k + rank) sources.setdefault(doc_id, []).append((name, rank)) fused = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]) if top_n: fused = fused[:top_n] return [{"doc_id": d, "rrf_score": round(s, 6), "found_by": sources[d]} for d, s in fused] ``` **`k=60` comes from Cormack et al.'s original paper and works without tuning.** It damps the influence of deep ranks — the difference between rank 1 and rank 2 matters far more than between rank 40 and rank 41, which matches how relevance actually behaves. **`found_by` is a genuinely useful diagnostic.** Documents retrieved by both methods are usually the strongest results, and if a large fraction of your final results come from only one source, the other is contributing little and you should investigate why. **Weighting** is worth tuning on your own labelled set. Technical corpora with many identifiers often want BM25 weighted at 1.2–1.5; conversational corpora favour dense. ```python class HybridRetriever: def __init__(self, bm25, vectorstore, corpus, weights=None, rrf_k=60): self.bm25, self.vs, self.corpus = bm25, vectorstore, corpus self.weights = weights or {"bm25": 1.0, "dense": 1.0} self.rrf_k = rrf_k def search(self, query, k=10, candidates=50): bm25_hits = [str(i) for i, _ in self.bm25.search(tokenize(query), k=candidates)] res = self.vs.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=candidates, include=["metadatas"]) dense_hits = [m["doc_index"] for m in res["metadatas"][0]] fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion( {"bm25": bm25_hits, "dense": dense_hits}, weights=self.weights, k=self.rrf_k, top_n=k, ) return [{**self.corpus[int(f["doc_id"])], **f} for f in fused] ``` ##### Cross-encoder reranking The second architectural change, and usually the larger one. **Bi-encoders** — the embedding models from Day 33 — encode query and document *separately*. That independence is what makes them fast (embed the corpus once) and what limits their accuracy (the model never sees the pair together). **Cross-encoders** take `(query, document)` as a single input with full attention between them. Far more accurate; far too slow to run over a corpus. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph BI["Bi-encoder — retrieval"] Q1["query"] --> E1["encoder"] --> V1["vector"] D1["doc"] --> E2["encoder"] --> V2["vector"] V1 --> C["cosine"] V2 --> C end subgraph CROSS["Cross-encoder — reranking"] QD["[CLS] query [SEP] doc [SEP]"] --> E3["encoder
full cross-attention"] E3 --> S["relevance score"] end BI -.->|"1M docs in 20ms"| X["fast, approximate"] CROSS -.->|"30 docs in 120ms"| Y["slow, accurate"] ``` ```python from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder import numpy as np class Reranker: def __init__(self, model_name="BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3", max_length=512, device="cuda"): self.model = CrossEncoder(model_name, max_length=max_length, device=device) def rerank(self, query, candidates, top_k=5, min_score=None, batch_size=32): if not candidates: return [] pairs = [(query, c["text"]) for c in candidates] scores = self.model.predict(pairs, batch_size=batch_size, show_progress_bar=False) for c, s in zip(candidates, scores): c["rerank_score"] = float(s) ranked = sorted(candidates, key=lambda c: -c["rerank_score"]) if min_score is not None: ranked = [c for c in ranked if c["rerank_score"] >= min_score] return ranked[:top_k] ``` **Model choices:** | Model | Size | Speed | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | `cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` | 22M | Very fast | English, good baseline | | `BAAI/bge-reranker-base` | 278M | Fast | Strong general purpose | | **`BAAI/bge-reranker-v2-m3`** | 568M | Moderate | **Multilingual, includes Indic** | | `jinaai/jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual` | 278M | Fast | Multilingual, efficient | | Cohere Rerank 3 | API | Fast | Excellent, paid | For Indian-language corpora, `bge-reranker-v2-m3` is the practical default — it handles Devanagari, Tamil, and code-mixed text where English-only rerankers fail badly. **The `min_score` threshold doubles as a relevance gate.** If nothing clears it, you have detected a retrieval failure and can refuse rather than answer from weak context — Day 35's grounding discipline, enforced at the retrieval layer. ##### ColBERT and late interaction The middle ground between the two paradigms. **ColBERT** (Khattab & Zaharia, 2020) encodes every *token* independently, then scores with MaxSim: $$S(q, d) = \sum_{i \in q} \max_{j \in d} \; E_{q_i} \cdot E_{d_j}$$ Each query token finds its best-matching document token; the scores sum. ```python import torch def maxsim_score(query_embeddings, doc_embeddings, doc_mask=None): """query: (Nq, D), doc: (Nd, D), both L2-normalised.""" sim = query_embeddings @ doc_embeddings.T # (Nq, Nd) if doc_mask is not None: sim = sim.masked_fill(~doc_mask.unsqueeze(0), -1e4) return sim.max(dim=1).values.sum().item() ``` **Why it is better than a bi-encoder:** token-level matching preserves fine-grained detail that a single pooled vector loses. A query token `WH-4471` can match that exact token in the document. **Why it is cheaper than a cross-encoder:** document embeddings are precomputed. Only the MaxSim is at query time. **The cost is storage.** Instead of one vector per document you store one per token — typically 100–300× more. PLAID and ColBERTv2 mitigate this with residual compression, bringing it to roughly 20–30× a single-vector index. **Where it fits:** as a first-stage retriever when you need better recall than a bi-encoder and cannot afford to rerank thousands of candidates. In practice most teams use bi-encoder plus cross-encoder because the tooling is simpler. ##### The full stack ```python class HybridRerankRetriever: """BM25 + dense → RRF → cross-encoder rerank.""" def __init__(self, bm25, vectorstore, corpus, reranker, bm25_weight=1.0, dense_weight=1.0, rrf_k=60): self.bm25, self.vs, self.corpus = bm25, vectorstore, corpus self.reranker = reranker self.weights = {"bm25": bm25_weight, "dense": dense_weight} self.rrf_k = rrf_k def search(self, query, k=5, candidates=30, min_rerank_score=None): import time timings = {} t0 = time.perf_counter() bm25_hits = [str(i) for i, _ in self.bm25.search(tokenize(query), k=candidates)] timings["bm25_ms"] = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000 t0 = time.perf_counter() res = self.vs.query(query_texts=[query], n_results=candidates, include=["metadatas"]) dense_hits = [m["doc_index"] for m in res["metadatas"][0]] timings["dense_ms"] = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000 fused = reciprocal_rank_fusion( {"bm25": bm25_hits, "dense": dense_hits}, weights=self.weights, k=self.rrf_k, top_n=candidates) pool = [{**self.corpus[int(f["doc_id"])], **f} for f in fused] t0 = time.perf_counter() final = self.reranker.rerank(query, pool, top_k=k, min_score=min_rerank_score) timings["rerank_ms"] = (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000 return {"results": final, "timings": timings, "candidates_considered": len(pool)} ``` ##### Measuring with nDCG Recall@k treats all retrieved relevant documents equally. **nDCG** accounts for graded relevance and position — the right answer at rank 1 is worth more than at rank 5. $$\text{DCG@k} = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \frac{2^{rel_i} - 1}{\log_2(i + 1)}, \qquad \text{nDCG@k} = \frac{\text{DCG@k}}{\text{IDCG@k}}$$ ```python import numpy as np def dcg_at_k(relevances, k): rel = np.asarray(relevances[:k], dtype=float) if rel.size == 0: return 0.0 discounts = np.log2(np.arange(2, rel.size + 2)) return float(((2 ** rel - 1) / discounts).sum()) def ndcg_at_k(retrieved_ids, relevance_map, k=10): """relevance_map: {doc_id: grade}, grade 0-3.""" rels = [relevance_map.get(d, 0) for d in retrieved_ids[:k]] ideal = sorted(relevance_map.values(), reverse=True)[:k] idcg = dcg_at_k(ideal, k) return round(dcg_at_k(rels, k) / idcg, 4) if idcg > 0 else 0.0 def evaluate_retriever(retriever, eval_set, k=10): """eval_set: [{'query': str, 'relevance': {doc_id: grade}}]""" ndcgs, recalls, mrrs, latencies = [], [], [], [] for item in eval_set: import time t0 = time.perf_counter() out = retriever.search(item["query"], k=k) latencies.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000) ids = [r["doc_id"] for r in (out["results"] if isinstance(out, dict) else out)] rel = item["relevance"] relevant = {d for d, g in rel.items() if g > 0} ndcgs.append(ndcg_at_k(ids, rel, k)) recalls.append(len(set(ids) & relevant) / max(len(relevant), 1)) mrrs.append(next((1 / r for r, d in enumerate(ids, 1) if d in relevant), 0.0)) return { f"nDCG@{k}": round(float(np.mean(ndcgs)), 4), f"recall@{k}": round(float(np.mean(recalls)), 4), "MRR": round(float(np.mean(mrrs)), 4), "p50_ms": round(float(np.percentile(latencies, 50)), 1), "p95_ms": round(float(np.percentile(latencies, 95)), 1), } ``` **Graded relevance requires labelling effort** — 0 for irrelevant through 3 for perfect. For 100 queries × 10 results that is 1,000 judgements, roughly four hours. It is the most valuable four hours available to a retrieval team, and it is why the Bengaluru team could tell that RRF helped by 13 points rather than guessing. ##### The latency-quality trade-off Your assignment. Reranking cost is linear in candidate count. ```python def rerank_sweep(retriever, reranker, eval_set, candidate_values=(10, 20, 30, 50, 100)): """How much does reranking more candidates buy, and cost?""" rows = [] for n in candidate_values: import time ndcgs, latencies = [], [] for item in eval_set: t0 = time.perf_counter() pool = retriever.search(item["query"], k=n) final = reranker.rerank(item["query"], pool, top_k=10) latencies.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000) ndcgs.append(ndcg_at_k([r["doc_id"] for r in final], item["relevance"], 10)) import numpy as np rows.append({ "candidates": n, "nDCG@10": round(float(np.mean(ndcgs)), 4), "p95_ms": round(float(np.percentile(latencies, 95)), 1), }) return rows ``` A representative sweep with `bge-reranker-v2-m3` on an A10G: | Candidates | nDCG@10 | p95 latency | Δ vs previous | |---|---|---|---| | 10 | 0.812 | 78ms | — | | 20 | 0.856 | 121ms | +0.044 / +43ms | | **30** | **0.874** | **164ms** | **+0.018 / +43ms** | | 50 | 0.883 | 251ms | +0.009 / +87ms | | 100 | 0.889 | 478ms | +0.006 / +227ms | **Thirty candidates is the knee of the curve.** Going to 100 buys 1.5 points for triple the latency. **Guidance by product type:** | Product | Latency budget | Candidates | Reranker | |---|---|---|---| | Interactive chat | < 200ms retrieval | 20–30 | Small/base | | Search UI | < 300ms | 30–50 | Base | | Async / batch | Seconds | 100–200 | Large | | High-stakes (legal, medical) | Seconds acceptable | 50–100 | Large + ensemble | **Optimisations worth knowing:** run BM25 and dense concurrently with `asyncio` (saves 20–40ms), quantize the reranker to INT8 (roughly 2× faster for under a point of nDCG), batch rerank requests across concurrent users, and cache reranker scores for repeated query-document pairs. ##### Common mistakes - **Two months on embedding models** when the gap is architectural — the Bengaluru story. - **Weighting BM25 and cosine scores directly** instead of fusing ranks. - **A `\w+` tokenizer** that shreds product codes and identifiers. - **Reranking 100 candidates** when 30 is the knee of the curve. - **English-only rerankers** on Indic or code-mixed corpora. - **No `min_score` gate**, so weak retrievals reach the generator. - **Measuring recall only**, missing that the right result ranks 8th. - **No graded relevance labels**, so nDCG is unavailable and improvements are guesses. - **Sequential BM25 and dense retrieval** when they can run concurrently. - **Reranking before fusion** rather than after — you want the reranker to see the union. - **Assuming hybrid always wins.** On purely conversational corpora with no identifiers, dense alone can match it. ##### Hands-on: build the stack, measure each layer Your practical task builds a hybrid retriever with RRF plus a cross-encoder and measures nDCG improvement. Measure three configurations on the same labelled set: dense only, hybrid, hybrid plus rerank. Log the `found_by` distribution in your fused results — if 90% of final results came from dense only, your BM25 tokenizer is probably shredding the identifiers that would have made it useful. The mini project builds a retrieval benchmark comparing the three configurations on a labelled query set. Invest the four hours in graded relevance labels; the resulting nDCG numbers are what let you make claims. Include at least 20% queries containing exact identifiers — product codes, error codes, clause numbers — because that is the query class where hybrid earns its keep, and an eval set of only natural-language questions will understate it. The assignment analyses the latency-quality trade-off of reranking top-k and recommends a production setting. Run the sweep on your own hardware, find your knee, then state a recommendation conditioned on a specific latency budget. "For our 200ms retrieval budget, rerank 30 candidates with `bge-reranker-base`, giving nDCG@10 of 0.87 at p95 164ms" is an engineering recommendation; a table alone is not. ##### Key takeaways - **Sparse and dense retrieval fail on disjoint query sets** — identifiers versus synonyms — which is why fusing them beats improving either one. - **RRF fuses by rank, not score**, which is what makes it work without per-corpus tuning; `k=60` needs no adjustment. - **Preserve hyphenated identifiers in your BM25 tokenizer.** A naive `\w+` throws away the exact-match advantage that justified adding BM25. - **Cross-encoder reranking is usually the single largest quality gain available**, and 30 candidates is typically the knee of the latency curve. - **Label graded relevance and measure nDCG.** Recall hides the difference between the right answer at rank 1 and at rank 8, which is exactly what reranking fixes.
practical_task_reference: Build a hybrid retriever (BM25 + dense) with RRF and add a cross-encoder reranker, measuring nDCG improvements.
mini_project_reference: Create a retrieval-quality benchmark comparing dense-only, hybrid, and hybrid+rerank on a labeled query set.
assignment_reference: Analyze the latency vs quality tradeoff of reranking top-k values and recommend a production setting.
